title: How does predicate pushdown work with Parquet specifically — (1) min/max statistics per column chunk at row-group and page level allow skipping irrelevant row groups, (2) dictionary filtering checks if the filter value exists in the dictionary page, (3) bloom filters provide probabilistic existence checks for high-cardinality columns — and why is sorted data important for min/max effectiveness?
shortTitle: Predicate pushdown with Parquet — min/max statistics, dictionary filtering, bloom filters

s1_definition.profdef: Parquet implements predicate pushdown through three complementary data-skipping mechanisms. Min/max statistics are stored per column chunk at the row-group and page level, so the reader can skip any block whose min/max range cannot satisfy the predicate. Dictionary filtering uses the dictionary page of an encoded column to check whether a filter value exists at all in a block, skipping the block if it does not. Bloom filters are compact probabilistic structures that answer "definitely not present" or "possibly present" for high-cardinality columns where min/max ranges are too wide to help. Min/max effectiveness depends heavily on sort order, because sorted data produces tight, non-overlapping ranges per block.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India's archive has three ways to avoid opening boxes. Each box has a label saying the smallest and largest account balance inside (min/max) — if you want balances above a lakh and the box tops out at fifty thousand, skip it. Each box also has an index card listing the distinct transaction types inside (dictionary) — if "wire transfer" is not on the card, skip the box. And each box has a quick fingerprint scanner (bloom filter) that can say "this account id is definitely not in here." If the boxes were filled in sorted order by balance, the min/max labels are tight and precise; if filled randomly, every box spans the whole range and the labels become useless.
s1_definition.oneliner: Parquet skips blocks using min/max ranges, dictionary membership, and bloom filters — and sorting the data makes min/max ranges tight enough to actually skip blocks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Parquet implements predicate pushdown through three complementary data-skipping mechanisms. Min/max statistics are stored per column chunk at the row-group and page level, so the reader can skip any block whose min/max range cannot satisfy the predicate. Dictionary filtering uses the dictionary page of an encoded column to check whether a filter value exists at all in a block, skipping the block if it does not. Bloom filters are compact probabilistic structures that answer "definitely not present" or "possibly present" for high-cardinality columns where min/max ranges are too wide to help. Min/max effectiveness depends heavily on sort order, because sorted data produces tight, non-overlapping ranges per block.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India's archive has three ways to avoid opening boxes. Each box has a label saying the smallest and largest account balance inside (min/max) — if you want balances above a lakh and the box tops out at fifty thousand, skip it. Each box also has an index card listing the distinct transaction types inside (dictionary) — if "wire transfer" is not on the card, skip the box. And each box has a quick fingerprint scanner (bloom filter) that can say "this account id is definitely not in here." If the boxes were filled in sorted order by balance, the min/max labels are tight and precise; if filled randomly, every box spans the whole range and the labels become useless.

**One line to remember:** Parquet skips blocks using min/max ranges, dictionary membership, and bloom filters — and sorting the data makes min/max ranges tight enough to actually skip blocks.

sections.s2_technical:
Min/max statistics are the first and most common mechanism. A Parquet file is split into row groups, each row group into column chunks, and each column chunk into pages. At the row-group level and the page level, Parquet stores the minimum and maximum value of each column. When Spark pushes a predicate like amount greater than one lakh, the reader compares it to each row group's max for amount; if the max is below one lakh, no row in the group can match, so the entire group is skipped without decompression. The same check runs at the finer page level, so even within a surviving row group only the relevant pages are decoded.

Dictionary filtering is the second mechanism and works for equality predicates. Parquet often dictionary-encodes a column, storing the distinct values once in a dictionary page and then storing small integer codes per row. For an equality filter like txnType equals wire, the reader can inspect the dictionary page of the block and, if wire is not in the dictionary, conclude no row in that block matches and skip it. This is powerful for low-to-medium cardinality columns that are dictionary-encoded, because checking the dictionary is far cheaper than scanning the values.

Bloom filters are the third mechanism, designed for high-cardinality columns where min/max is useless. A bloom filter is a compact bitset computed by hashing each value into several bits. To test a value, you hash it and check those bits: if any is zero, the value is definitely not present and the block is skipped; if all are set, the value is possibly present and the block is read. Bloom filters never give false negatives, only false positives, so they are safe for skipping. They shine for things like equality filters on transaction id or account id, where the value range is so wide that every block's min/max spans almost everything.

The crucial point about sort order ties it together. Min/max statistics only help if the ranges per block are tight and mostly non-overlapping. If the data is sorted by the filter column, block zero might hold amounts zero to ten thousand, block one ten thousand to twenty thousand, and so on, so a filter on a value cleanly isolates a few blocks. If the data is unsorted, every block holds a random spread from near-zero to near-maximum, so every block's min/max range covers the whole domain and no block can ever be skipped — the statistics exist but are worthless. That is why people sort or Z-order data on frequently filtered columns before writing Parquet.

A senior-level nuance is that these mechanisms layer: min/max and dictionary are on by default, while bloom filters must be explicitly enabled per column at write time because they cost space, so you enable them only for high-cardinality columns you filter by equality. And all of this depends on the predicate being pushable in the first place, which you verify through the plan's PushedFilters.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India queries years of Parquet transactions for amounts above one lakh. If the data was written sorted by amount, the min/max statistics let the reader skip every block topping out below one lakh. This is min/max pushdown, effective because of the sort.

Problem 2 — A query filters on transaction type equals wire. Because type is dictionary-encoded, the reader checks each block's dictionary and skips blocks where wire is absent. This is dictionary filtering.

Problem 3 — A query looks up a single transaction id in a huge table. Transaction id is so high cardinality that every block's min/max spans the whole range, so min/max cannot skip anything. A bloom filter on transaction id lets the reader skip most blocks with a definitely-not-present answer. This is the bloom filter case.

The demo models blocks with min/max, dictionaries, and bloom filters, runs the three filters, and reports which blocks are skipped by which mechanism, contrasting sorted versus unsorted min/max effectiveness.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four Parquet blocks written sorted by amount, with amount ranges, a type dictionary, and bloom membership for transaction ids.

Step 1: For the min/max filter amount greater than one lakh, the reader checks each block's max. Block 0 tops at 25000 and block 1 at 75000, both below one lakh, so both skip. Block 2 tops at 150000 and block 3 at 900000, so both are read. Because the data is sorted, these ranges are tight and skipping is precise.

Step 2: For the dictionary filter type equals wire, the reader checks each block's dictionary. Blocks 0 and 1 do not contain wire, so they skip; blocks 2 and 3 do, so they read.

Step 3: For the bloom filter transaction id equals TX-6, the reader tests each block's bloom. Only block 2 possibly contains TX-6; blocks 0, 1, and 3 return definitely-not-present and skip. This works even though transaction id is high cardinality and min/max would be useless.

Step 4: The demo warns that if the data were unsorted, every block's amount min/max would span the full range and min/max could skip nothing — the reason sorting matters.

Final output:

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Parquet blocks (sorted by amount)
    B0[0..25k]  B1[25k..75k]  B2[75k..150k]  B3[150k..900k]
    │
    ├─ amount > 100k  (min/max)
    │     B0 SKIP  B1 SKIP  B2 READ  B3 READ
    │
    ├─ type = 'wire'  (dictionary)
    │     B0 SKIP(no wire)  B2 READ(has wire)  B3 READ
    │
    ▼ txnId = 'TX-6'  (bloom, high cardinality)
       B0 SKIP  B1 SKIP  B2 READ(maybe)  B3 SKIP
       (min/max useless here → bloom saves the day)

  UNSORTED: every block min..max = 0..900k → 0 skips by min/max
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Parquet implements predicate pushdown through three layered data-skipping mechanisms, and knowing all three shows depth. The first is min/max statistics. A Parquet file is divided into row groups, column chunks, and pages, and at both the row-group and page level it stores the minimum and maximum of each column. When Spark pushes a filter, the reader compares it to those ranges and skips any block whose range cannot satisfy the predicate, without decompressing it. The second is dictionary filtering, which helps equality predicates: when a column is dictionary-encoded, the reader inspects the block's dictionary page, and if the filter value is not in the dictionary, no row in that block can match, so it skips the block. The third is bloom filters, compact probabilistic bitsets for high-cardinality columns; testing a value gives either definitely-not-present, which lets the block be skipped safely because bloom filters never produce false negatives, or possibly-present, which means read it.

The reason the question stresses sort order is that min/max is only useful when the per-block ranges are tight and mostly non-overlapping. If the data is sorted by the filter column, one block holds a narrow slice of values, so a filter cleanly isolates a few blocks. If the data is unsorted, every block holds a random spread covering almost the whole range, so every block's min/max spans everything and nothing can ever be skipped — the statistics exist but are worthless. That is why we sort or Z-order on frequently filtered columns before writing.

At the National Bank of India this was exactly how we tuned our Parquet transaction tables. We sorted by amount and date so amount and date filters could skip most blocks by min/max, we relied on dictionary filtering for low-cardinality columns like transaction type, and we enabled bloom filters specifically on the high-cardinality transaction id so point lookups could skip blocks that min/max could never help with. The rule I give in interviews is that min/max and dictionary skipping are on by default, bloom filters must be enabled per column at write time because they cost space, and sorting the data on your filter columns is what makes min/max actually skip blocks rather than merely exist.
